claimText: The default match-score threshold for OpenSanctions-backed screening (above which a candidate is surfaced as a match) is 0.7, and the default algorithm is calibrated to be used with that value.

source.title: OpenSanctions API: Tuning the Matching System

claimText: A match query is processed in two stages: first a search index locates candidate results optimized for recall (retrieval), then those candidates are evaluated against the query using the configured matching algorithm (scoring).

source.title: OpenSanctions API: Tuning the Matching System

claimText: OpenSanctions' regression-v1 matching algorithm scores candidates across exactly 18 named features (e.g. name_match, name_token_overlap, name_levenshtein, dob_matches, dob_year_matches, dob_year_disjoint, identifier_match, org_identifier_match, address_match, gender_mismatch, country_mismatch, and others), confirmed by manual count of the published feature table, not name similarity alone.

source.title: OpenSanctions Matcher: Supported Matching Algorithms

claimText: The name-based and name-qualified algorithms compare names using Jaro-Winkler string similarity combined with Soundex phonetic matching, are both deprecated in favour of the ofac (OFACMatcher) algorithm, and OpenSanctions' own documentation states neither reaches parity with OFAC's public Sanctions List Search tool.

source.title: OpenSanctions Matcher: Deprecated Matching Algorithms

claimText: A separate algorithm (ofac / OFACMatcher) is reverse-engineered from OFAC's own scoring FAQ (FAQ #249) and parity fixtures captured against the live public tool, specifically to emulate sanctionssearch.ofac.treas.gov's behaviour, distinct from the deprecated name-based and name-qualified algorithms.

source.title: OpenSanctions Matcher: ofac Algorithm

claimText: logic-v2 is a deterministic, rule-based matching algorithm whose name matcher uses curated, multilingual cultural reference data for cross-language and cross-script matching, and OpenSanctions' own API tuning documentation recommends pinning to logic-v2 for new integrations.

source.title: OpenSanctions Matcher (logic-v2) and API Tuning documentation

claimText: Two individuals named Khalid Mehmood on Pakistan's proscribed persons list, sharing the same name, country, and sanctions programme but different national ID numbers (ending 9885 and 0181) and different father's names (Muhammad Khan and Haji Muhammad), were assigned a 0.98 match score by a rule-based (RegressionV1/Nomenklatura) baseline in a February 2026 academic benchmark.

claimText: A 34-year-old man in Amsterdam used face-swap software on stolen ID photos (partly obtained via a fake rental listing scam) to open 46 fraudulent accounts at ABN AMRO through the bank's mobile onboarding flow. The fraud surfaced when one application's ID photo showed a woman while the accompanying selfie showed a man. Convicted June 2026, sentenced to 30 months (6 suspended), ordered to repay over EUR13,000. The specific ECLI case citation could not be independently verified (rechtspraak.nl blocks automated access; no secondary source's rendered text contained it), so no ECLI number is asserted in the guide, only the Rechtspraak.nl news page itself is cited. The account count is reported inconsistently across sources: 46 (DutchNews.nl, used throughout this guide) versus 47 (security.nl, Dutch-language reporting); not reconciled, logged here rather than silently picking one.

source.title: 2,5 jaar cel voor oplichten bank met deepfake-technologie / Man opened 46 bank accounts using deepfakes and stolen IDs

claimText: An AI agent is software that can interpret a goal, break it into steps, and act on digital services with limited human input at each step, rather than requiring explicit approval for every action. Modern payment systems are built on deterministic logic; agentic AI is probabilistic, the same instruction can produce a different action on a different run.

source.title: How Agentic AI Will Reshape Payments, IMF Notes 2026, Issue 004
source.publisher: International Monetary Fund (Davidovic, S. and Tourpe, H.)

claimText: The FCA's 2026 Payments Regulatory Priorities report states the regulator will consider whether change or development of regulation is needed to support agentic AI payments, a departure from its usual posture of applying existing rules to new technology. Confirmed by direct verbatim quote from page 7 of the primary source, under the heading "Modernise payments regulation": "This will include considering whether change or development of regulation is needed to support agentic AI payments." Context worth noting so the record doesn't overstate prominence: this is one bullet point among several other priorities in a routine annual Payments Regulatory Priorities report, not a standalone or headline announcement.

source.title: 2026 Payments Regulatory Priorities

claimText: Regulation 67 of the Payment Services Regulations 2017: a payment transaction is regarded as authorised by the payer only if the payer has given consent to the execution of the payment transaction (or a series of which it forms part).

source.title: The Payment Services Regulations 2017 (SI 2017/752), regulation 67

claimText: Regulation 76 of the Payment Services Regulations 2017: where an executed payment transaction was not authorised in accordance with regulation 67, the payment service provider must refund the amount to the payer by the end of the next business day, subject to a fraud-suspicion exception requiring notification under POCA 2002 s.333A(2).

source.title: The Payment Services Regulations 2017 (SI 2017/752), regulation 76

claimText: The CMA's Agentic AI and consumers publication states existing consumer protection law (including DMCC Act powers) applies to conduct by AI agents in the same way as human-generated conduct, businesses deploying AI agents are responsible for what those agents do; the publication does not resolve which specific party bears liability when an agent's decision causes harm.

source.title: Agentic AI and consumers

claimText: Google's Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) launched 16 September 2025 with 60+ launch partners including Mastercard, PayPal, Coinbase, and American Express. It defines a three-mandate chain (Intent, Cart, Payment) carried as W3C Verifiable Credentials, and its v0.2 release explicitly added Human Not Present payment support (the agent completes the full chain autonomously within the original Intent Mandate's boundaries, no further human confirmation).

source.title: Agent Payments Protocol (AP2)

claimText: x402 is Coinbase's open, HTTP-402-based standard for internet-native stablecoin micropayments, enabling machine-to-machine and AI-agent payments without login. Now under Linux Foundation governance, backed by Google, Visa, Mastercard, Stripe, AWS, and Circle.

source.title: Introducing x402: a new standard for internet-native payments

claimText: Legal commentary (not settled law): existing regulations struggle to distinguish unauthorised use from user negligence when an agent hallucinates or misdirects funds, and the current framework does not allocate liability between PISPs, account servicing PSPs, and AI technology providers; whether liability sits with the consumer, the AI developer, the PSP, or the merchant remains genuinely unclear. This is a narrower, more evenly-balanced framing than an earlier draft of this guide assumed (which leaned toward PSP liability as the likely outcome); corrected to match what the source actually says before publication.

source.title: Agentic AI in payments: Key regulatory considerations
source.publisher: Taylor Wessing (legal commentary, not primary regulation)

claimText: American Express launched its Agentic Commerce Experiences (ACE) developer kit on 14 April 2026, alongside an industry-first Agent Purchase Protection commitment covering eligible erroneous purchases made by registered, verified AI agents on its network. The model requires prior cardholder authentication before payment credentials are issued to a verified agent.

source.title: American Express Debuts Agentic Commerce Experiences (ACE) Developer Kit and Announces Industry-First Protection for Registered Agent Purchases

claimText: UKGC's 2026 money laundering and terrorist financing risk assessment (Section 9, Betting remote), published 30 July 2026, rates inadequate due diligence on white-label partnerships as high likelihood x high impact (high overall risk), unchanged in rating from the prior assessment (new wording only).
